## Are condo fees worth it in Myrtle Beach?
Condo fees are usually worth it, because owners pay together through the fee for what no one owner could buy alone.

- The building's insurance South Carolina law requires a condo association to insure the property. Each owner may still insure their own unit.

- The roof In a condo, the roof belongs to all the owners together, and its repair is a shared expense. Owners of a one-family house in the South Atlantic states, which include South Carolina, who replaced a roof paid a middle of more than $10,000.

- A policy lenders accept For a loan sold to Fannie Mae, the building's deductible may be no more than 5 percent of its coverage. When it is charged per unit, the limit is $50,000 a unit. If the policy falls outside those limits, fewer of your buyers can get a loan there. Our page on the building's policy and your own explains both.

Our page about Myrtle Beach HOA fees explains why condo fees are high here. The fee in each community is in our list of HOA fees in 382 neighborhoods . Fees building by building are on our oceanfront condo buildings page.

## Do HOAs increase property value in Myrtle Beach?
Not in asking prices. Here, newer houses with an HOA fee list for less a square foot than houses without one. Of houses for sale built in 2000 or later in Horry County ZIP codes, those with a fee list for a middle of about $205 a square foot. Those with no fee list for about $274.
The house with no fee also sits on more land: about half an acre, against about a fifth of an acre with a fee.

## What do you give up in an HOA?
In an HOA you give up room, some freedom and some say over the money. In return, every neighbor follows the same rules you do.
Whether the dues come off your taxes is on our page on HOA fees and taxes .

- Room for a boat or an RV Our listing feed covers the Grand Strand from Pawleys Island into North Carolina. In it, about 3 in 100 houses for sale with an HOA fee list parking for an RV or a boat. With no fee, about 3 in 10 do. Houses with a fee list a boat ramp more often, 9 in 100 against 2. Our page on homes with no HOA shows where those houses are.

- Things you cannot build or park Each community above has rules against something: a private pool, a shed or a boat in the driveway. The biggest mistake we see buyers from New York make is not checking that the community's rules fit how they live. That means the HOA rules on boats, golf carts, rentals and pools.

- No cap in state law South Carolina's HOA law and condo law put no cap on dues, on a special assessment or on a fine . The limits are in each community's own recorded rules and bylaws. The Farm's recorded rules cap a yearly increase in the base fee at 20 percent. More on how much an HOA can raise dues .

- A low fee can mean thin savings If an HOA saves too little for repairs, owners can face a special assessment later, a one-time bill to each owner. Our page on HOA reserves covers how much an HOA should save.

### What do owners here complain to the state about?
Of the concerns the state names, the most common, in 36 of 100 complaints, was that the HOA did not follow or enforce its own rules. Maintenance and repairs came next, in 30 of 100.

## Can an HOA Fine You in SC? There's No Legal Cap | Chapter3
URL: https://chapter3realty.com/hoa/violations-and-fines/
Summary: South Carolina law puts no cap on HOA fines and requires no hearing first. What you can be fined for sits in your recorded documents, and where to fight a fine.

Home / HOA Guide / Violations and Fines
Violations and fines

# Can your HOA fine you? In South Carolina, there is no legal cap.
By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge, 30+ years on the Grand Strand · Updated November 12, 2026
South Carolina law does not cap HOA fines and gives you no hearing and no notice period before one. Your association's power to fine comes from its recorded documents.
Have us read the rules Call 854.333.2135

WHAT THE LAW SAYS

## State law does not cap HOA fines
South Carolina has one law written for homeowners associations. It covers recording, budget notice, document access and small claims court. It says nothing about fines. The word fine does not appear in it. It does not appear in the state's condo law either.
There is no legal cap on what you can be charged. There is no legal right to a hearing. There is no set notice period before a fine lands. Every limit that applies to you is written into your own association's documents.
You may have read that South Carolina caps fines at $100 and gives you 14 days notice before a hearing. That is not law here. It came from a bill that was filed and never passed. Do not count on it.

YOUR OWN DOCUMENTS

## Your fine comes from your own paperwork
Because state law is silent, your association's power to fine you sits in its own documents. There are three pieces and they are not the same thing.
The declaration, sometimes called the master deed, is the recorded document that creates the association. People also call it the covenants or the CC&Rs. It says what the association can enforce against your unit. The bylaws say how the board runs itself, including any hearing step the board chose to give you. The rules are what the board adopts on its own, and they change most often.
Ask for all three before you buy, and ask for the rules with the date each one was adopted. Most associations hand the package over in about three days. That is what we usually see, not a promise. Get the request in early so a slow response does not push your closing.
Send the package to Chapter3 and we will read it with you. It goes into our analysis tool the day it arrives and a person reads the result. Call us or use the form on this site.

- &#10003; The declaration or master deed. Says what the association can enforce against your unit.

- &#10003; The bylaws. Say how the board runs itself, including whether you get a hearing.

- &#10003; The rules. The board adopts these on its own, so ask for the date each one was adopted.

- &#10003; Open violations. Have the seller get this from the association: any open violation on the unit, and what it costs to clear it.

Have us read the rules Call 854.333.2135

THE RECORDING CHECK

## A rule has to be recorded to stick
The state does control recording, and few owners check it. With a few exceptions, association documents have to be recorded at the county records office to be enforced. In Horry County that office is the Register of Deeds.
Rules carry a second deadline. A new rule takes effect the moment the board adopts it. But it has to be recorded by January 10 of the following year. If it was not, it stops being enforceable. The same goes for any change to a rule, so a rule can bind you one year and lose its force the next.
That gives you something concrete to do. Find the exact rule you are accused of breaking. Then look it up in the county recording index. The association's own copy of a rule does not prove it was recorded. Whether a missing recording defeats a particular fine is a question for a South Carolina attorney, so ask before you pay.

CONDOS

## In a condo the board sues you
If you are buying a condo, a different state law applies. Nothing in it lets a condo board fine anyone. The word fine never appears there either.
What that law gives the board instead is a lawsuit. You have to follow the bylaws, the rules adopted under them, and the covenants in the master deed. An owner who does not can be sued for money owed, or ordered by a court to stop.
The same door opens the other way. An owner who has been wronged can bring that action too. If your board is ignoring its own bylaws, you can sue to make it follow them. Talk to a South Carolina attorney before you file anything.
In a condo, a fine can only come from the recorded master deed, bylaws and rules. Read them before you buy, not after.
Have us read the rules Call 854.333.2135

IF YOU GET ONE

## Where to take a fine you think is wrong
Start in writing. Ask for the exact rule you broke, the date the board adopted it, the recording information for that rule, and the amount you owe. That request costs you nothing and it creates a record.
If that goes nowhere, there are two routes and neither is a sure thing. One is magistrates court, the state's small claims court. It can hear a claim for money up to $7,500, and a claim over a fine counts. It cannot hear a case that turns on who owns the property, and it can only order money. It is not where you get an order telling the association to back off. Circuit court can hear these cases as well.
The second route is a complaint to the state consumer agency. Know what that is before you spend time on it. The process is voluntary mediation. The agency cannot force your association to take part, cannot require an outcome and cannot decide the dispute.
If you are still buying, this is far easier to handle now. Have the seller provide any open violation or unpaid fine on the unit, with the payoff figure from the association. Then ask what the association charges at closing. Almost all of them charge something. A few months of dues up front is common, plus a document fee and a fee to open your account.
Chapter3 asks those questions before you are under contract. Call us or send the documents through this site and we will tell you what you are buying into.
This page is general information about South Carolina law. It is not legal advice. Take a fine or a violation notice to a South Carolina attorney.

- &#10003; Ask in writing first. The rule, the date the board adopted it, and the payoff figure.

- &#10003; Money only. Small claims court can order a sum. It cannot order the board to stop.

- &#10003; Ask before closing. An unresolved violation can become yours once the deed changes hands.

Common questions

## Violations and Fines FAQ

### Is there a limit on how much an HOA can fine you in South Carolina?
No. State law sets no cap on HOA fines. The word fine does not appear in the state HOA law or in the condo law. The $100 cap you see quoted online came from a bill that never passed. Any limit that applies to you is in your own documents.

### Does an HOA have to give you notice or a hearing before it fines you?
Not under state law. There is no notice period before a fine, no right to a hearing and no review panel. If you get any of that, it is because your association's own bylaws give it to you. Read the bylaws to find out whether they do.

### Can you fight an HOA fine in South Carolina?
You can try two routes. Small claims court can hear a money claim up to $7,500, but it cannot order the association to stop. A complaint to the state consumer agency is voluntary mediation only. Take a real dispute to a South Carolina attorney.

### Can an HOA fine you over a rule that was never recorded?
Recording is what makes a rule enforceable. A rule has to be recorded by January 10 of the year after the board adopts or changes it. Look up the rule you are accused of breaking in the county recording index, then take what you find to a South Carolina attorney.

### What happens if you do not pay an HOA fine?
It depends on your documents. In a condo, unpaid assessments become a lien, which is a legal claim recorded against the unit itself, and it outranks most other claims. Whether a fine can become a lien depends on your own paperwork. Read it before you buy.

## South Carolina HOA Estoppel Letter: Fees, Who Pays, How Long
URL: https://chapter3realty.com/hoa/estoppel-and-transfer-fees/
Summary: What an HOA estoppel letter is, why you have to ask for one, what it caps, and what the HOA will charge you at closing in South Carolina.

Home / HOA Guide / Estoppel and Fees
What the HOA charges at closing

# HOA Estoppel Letters and Transfer Fees in South Carolina
By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge, 30+ years on the Grand Strand · Updated November 12, 2026
An estoppel letter is the HOA's written statement of what the current owner owes. In most South Carolina condos you have a right to one, but only if you ask.
Ask us what is owed Call 854.333.2135

WHAT IT IS

## The letter is the HOA payoff figure
An estoppel letter is a written statement from the HOA. It says what the owner owes on that unit, as of one date. The closing attorney uses the number to pay the HOA out of the sale money. Some HOAs call it a statement of amounts due. It is the same document.
The HOA only has to write it when a buyer asks. Nobody offers it. Not the HOA, not the manager, not the seller. If nobody asks, nobody writes it. Put the request in writing, early, to whoever keeps the HOA's books.
In most condos you have a right to that statement. In a neighborhood of houses or townhouses you may not. There you get only what your contract gives you, so write the payoff figure into the contract as a term. Ask for these five things either way.

- &#10003; Regular dues. The balance through a set date, and what comes due next.

- &#10003; Special assessments. What was charged, how much is still unpaid, and whether it can be paid in parts.

- &#10003; Anything else the HOA says is owed. On the same statement, not in a side email.

- &#10003; The as of date. Closing dates move, and the statement speaks as of one day.

- &#10003; Any fee due at closing, and which side the HOA plans to bill for it.

WHY IT MATTERS

## Old dues follow the unit to you
If the seller owes back dues, you owe them once you buy. The debt sticks to the unit, not to the person who ran it up. The HOA can come after you for the whole amount. You can then go after the seller for your money, but that is a lawsuit you did not plan on.
Asking for the statement is what protects you. Once you have it, what the HOA can make you pay is capped at the figure on it. That cap is the reason to ask. No request, no cap.
The unpaid balance also comes out of the sale price at closing, ahead of most other charges. If it is large, it can eat what the seller walks away with, and that can blow up your deal late. Send us the address of the unit you are looking at. We will request the statement, read what comes back, and tell you what you would be walking into.
Ask us what is owed Call 854.333.2135

TIMING AND COST

## Nobody has to hurry, so ask early
South Carolina sets no deadline for the statement. There is no turnaround time, no penalty for being slow, and no limit on what the HOA or its manager can charge to write it. The only rule is that they have to give it when a buyer asks.
HOAs and their managers tend to take about three days to release documents, and some take longer. That is what we see. We do not control that timing.
The only pressure in this process is the lead time you give yourself. Ask at the start of your due diligence, not the week of closing. Ask what it costs and who gets the bill. State law does not say who pays, which makes it a contract term, and whoever the contract names is the one who pays. This page is general information, not legal advice. Have a South Carolina real estate attorney read your contract wording.

FEES AT CLOSING

## What the HOA charges you at closing
Expect a bill from the HOA at closing. It is usually a few months of dues up front, a document fee, and a fee to open your account on the HOA's books. No South Carolina law caps these fees or says what they are. Ask the HOA or its manager for its own figures in writing, early, so nothing on the settlement statement is a surprise.
Some communities also charge a transfer fee when a unit changes hands. A fee paid to the HOA itself, and spent on the community, is normal and enforceable here. A fee that gets passed to an outside company is a different thing. South Carolina will not enforce one of those recorded since 2012, and older ones can still stand. Many lenders will not lend on a home tied to a fee like that either, so it can also be a financing problem. Have your attorney read the clause and find out where the money goes.
There is no cap on any of it and no rule on who pays. That makes it one more thing you negotiate. Get the split written into the contract before you sign, and get the HOA's own figure rather than an estimate from anyone else.
Ask us what is owed Call 854.333.2135

APPROVAL AND FIRST REFUSAL

## Approval rights come from the documents
State law does not let an HOA approve or reject a buyer, and it does not give an HOA a right of first refusal. A right of first refusal is a clause that lets the HOA match your offer and take the unit instead of you.
If an HOA claims either power, it is written into the recorded declaration and bylaws. If it is not written there, it does not exist. Read both documents before you write the offer, and look for three things.
Ask for the HOA documents and the payoff statement the day you go under contract. We do this on every condo we sell. Send us the unit, and we will pull the documents, read them, and tell you what you are agreeing to while you still have time to walk.

- &#10003; Approval. Whether the HOA has to approve you, what it can ask you for, and how many days it gets.

- &#10003; First refusal. Whether the HOA can match your offer, and the days it has to decide.

- &#10003; The day count. A clause with no deadline can hold your closing open with nothing to push against, so build the days into your contract dates.

Common questions

## Estoppel and Fees FAQ

### What is an HOA estoppel letter in South Carolina?
It is a written statement from the HOA of what the current owner owes on the unit, good as of one date. The closing attorney uses that figure to pay the HOA out of the sale. The HOA only writes it when a buyer asks for it.

### Who pays for the estoppel letter, the buyer or the seller?
State law does not say. That makes it a contract term, so whoever the purchase agreement names is the one who pays. Ask the HOA what it charges and which side it plans to bill, then write the split into the contract before you sign.

### How long does an HOA have to send an estoppel letter?
There is no deadline in South Carolina and no penalty for being slow. The HOA has to give the statement when a buyer asks, and that is all the law says. We see HOAs take about three days to release documents, but that is a pattern, not a rule.

### Can I be made to pay the last owner's unpaid HOA dues?
In most condos, yes. The debt follows the unit, so the HOA can come after you for the seller's balance once you own it. Ask for the written statement of what is owed. What you can then be made to pay is capped at the figure on it.

### Are HOA transfer fees legal in South Carolina?
A fee paid to the HOA itself and spent on the community is enforceable. A fee that gets passed to an outside company usually is not, and it can make the home harder to finance. There is no cap on the amount and no rule on who pays.

## Developer-Controlled HOA Turnover in SC | Chapter3 Realty
URL: https://chapter3realty.com/hoa/developer-control-turnover/
Summary: South Carolina sets no HOA turnover deadline and no percentage-sold rule. The recorded documents decide. What to read before you buy in a new community.

Home / HOA Guide / Developer Control
Developer controlled HOAs

# Buying into a developer-controlled HOA South Carolina sets no turnover deadline
By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge, 30+ years on the Grand Strand · Updated November 12, 2026
Turnover is when the developer hands the HOA to an owner-elected board. South Carolina sets no deadline and no percentage sold; the recorded documents decide, and the developer wrote them.
Have us check control Call 854.333.2135

THE DIRECT ANSWER

## No law sets a turnover date
Turnover is the handover. The developer stops running the HOA and the owners elect their own board. South Carolina has no law that says when that must happen. No deadline. No percentage of homes sold. No duty to hand over at all.
The recorded documents decide. The declaration and the bylaws set the trigger, and the developer wrote both before a single owner existed. Those documents call the developer the declarant, so that is the word to search for. Look for what ends developer control. If nothing ends it, that is your answer.
The developer can also write advantages in for itself. Its votes can count for more than yours. It can appoint some board seats instead of letting owners elect them. One rule protects you. Governing documents have to be recorded at the county land records office to be enforceable, so they are public and you need nobody's permission to read them. Our page on South Carolina HOA laws covers the rest.

THE MONEY

## The dues quote may be an estimate
Before turnover, the dues figure you are quoted can be a forecast instead of a full year of real bills. A forecast written by the party selling you the home is not the same as twelve months of paid invoices. You are not an owner yet, so you cannot request association records. The seller can. Have the seller provide the budget and the dues history before you make an offer.
Ask for the reserves the same way. Reserves are the savings account the community keeps for big repairs. If the account is short and a roof or an elevator fails, the money gets raised from owners instead. That is a special assessment, and it can run into thousands per home. Our pages on what HOA fees cover and reserves and reserve studies show you how to read the numbers.
There is usually something to pay at closing too. A few months of dues up front is common, plus a document fee and an account setup fee. Amounts vary by community, so ask early. Tell us which community you are looking at and we will get the budget, the reserve study and the dues history from the seller before you make an offer.

- &#10003; Budget or projection. Have the seller provide the current budget, then check whether the dues figure comes from real bills or from an estimate.

- &#10003; Reserve study and balance. Ask the seller for the study, when it was done, and what sits in the account today.

- &#10003; Unsold lots. Read what the developer pays on the homes it still owns, and whether it pays the full amount.

- &#10003; Who can raise dues. Read the assessment section for a cap, a limit on yearly rises, and who votes.

- &#10003; Notice before a raise. Ask how much warning owners get before a dues increase is voted. State law requires 48 hours only from an HOA that is not a nonprofit corporation. For a nonprofit HOA, the bylaws decide.

Have us check control Call 854.333.2135

THE LOAN

## Developer control slows the loan down
While the developer still runs the HOA, most lenders treat the community as new, even if it looks finished and nearly sold out. A new community gets a longer, deeper review of the association itself. The lender reads the budget, the reserves, the insurance and any lawsuits.
That review has a shelf life. On a community the developer still controls it expires sooner, and on a slow build it can run out and have to be done a second time before you close. Start it early. If a community cannot pass, there are lenders who work outside those rules. Our page on non-warrantable condos explains that route.
You will also read that a set percentage of homes has to be sold before turnover. That is not a state rule. Those percentages come from mortgage rules about where a lender will lend. They are conditions on a loan, not duties on a developer. Ask us, and a loan officer at our preferred lender will tell you what a lender needs on a specific community before you write an offer.

AFTER THE HANDOVER

## Turnover is when owners get to decide
A Grand Strand community moved from builder control to an owner-elected board. The obvious ideas came first. A pool. A dog park. A barbecue area. Then the new board read the numbers.
The money went somewhere else. It was spent on preventing storm damage, chosen in close work with the insurers. The next renewal came in under a 5 percent rise while comparable communities nearby saw far larger ones, and owners were told exactly why. The board also renegotiated the lawn care contract to help absorb the insurance cost.
Turnover is where dues can jump. It is also the point where owners finally get to hold them down. Which one you get depends on whether the new board reads the numbers before it spends.
Have us check control Call 854.333.2135

BEFORE YOU SIGN

## Get the documents before you sign
The right to demand records from an HOA belongs to members, and a buyer under contract is not a member yet. Nothing hands you the budget or the rules before closing. The seller disclosure will not fill the gap either. A seller has to say whether there is an HOA, and is also allowed to answer that they make no representations. Most people who complain about their HOA never saw the documents before they bought.
Two things work. Pull the recorded documents at the county office yourself. Put a deadline in your contract for the association package, with the right to walk if the documents do not match what you were told. Associations usually take about three days to send one. Our page on which HOA documents to request lists each document and what it shows.
Send us the address and we will pull what is recorded, run the package through our document tool, and have a person read the output with you. Our Broker-in-Charge, Tim Nash, holds South Carolina real estate license 43182. We are not attorneys and this is not legal advice. Ask a South Carolina attorney about your rights.

- &#10003; The declaration, plus every recorded amendment. Amendments are where developer rights get extended.

- &#10003; The bylaws. This is where you find who runs the place and how board seats get filled.

- &#10003; The current budget and the latest reserve study. Have the seller ask the association whether the budget is actual or projected.

- &#10003; The dues history. Every increase since the first closing in the community.

Common questions

## Developer Control FAQ

### When does a developer have to turn over an HOA in South Carolina?
There is no deadline in state law. No date, no percentage sold, no duty to hand over at all. The recorded declaration and bylaws decide it. Read the declaration and every amendment, and look for what ends developer control. If nothing ends it, that is an answer too.

### What percentage of homes has to be sold before HOA turnover in SC?
None. South Carolina sets no percentage that triggers turnover. The percentages buyers read about come from mortgage rules, which decide where a lender will lend. They are conditions on a loan, not duties on a developer. Only the recorded documents set the trigger in your community.

### Can I get a mortgage on a condo when the developer still controls the HOA?
Usually yes, but expect a longer review. While the developer runs the association, most lenders treat the community as new and review the association in full. That review can expire on a slow build and have to be run again. Ask your lender to start it early.

### Will HOA dues go up after the developer turns over the community?
They can go either way, so ask two questions. Is the dues figure built from a full year of real bills or from an estimate, and has a reserve study been done. A short reserve account is the usual reason a special assessment shows up later.

### How do I get the HOA documents before I buy in a new community?
Use the county recording office and your contract. Governing documents have to be recorded to be enforceable, so they are public and anyone can read them. The right to demand records from the association belongs to members, and you are not one yet. Put a document deadline in the contract.

## Are HOA Fees Tax Deductible in South Carolina? | Chapter3
URL: https://chapter3realty.com/hoa/tax-deductible/
Summary: HOA fees on a home you live in are not deductible; on a rental they are. The rented share, second homes, special assessments, Schedule E and Grand Strand dues.

Home / HOA Guide / Tax deductible
HOA Guide

# Are HOA fees tax deductible in South Carolina? Not on the home you live in. Yes on the nights you rent it out.

- $0 of HOA fees deductible on a home you live in

- $7,800 a year deductible on a condo rented all year at the middle Horry County dues

- About 11 times a year of dues against the property tax on a Myrtle Beach condo its owner lives in

By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge · Updated November 14, 2026
On a Horry County condo with the middle HOA fees of $650 a month, the nights you rent it decide how much is deductible.

The short answer
HOA fees on a home you live in are not tax deductible. On a condo or house you rent out, the dues are a rental expense, taken off the rent on Schedule E, the IRS form for rental income.
If you rent it out and also stay there, you deduct the rented share. Divide the nights rented at a fair price by those nights plus your personal nights. The same rules on dues apply on the South Carolina return.

Looking at a condo? Get its dues and what they include before you offer.

## Are HOA fees tax deductible?
Only when the home is rented out. The IRS lists homeowners association (HOA) fees, condo fees and common charges with homeowners insurance, utilities and internet service as costs you cannot deduct on a home . On a rental, IRS Publication 527 lets you deduct dues paid for upkeep of the shared parts of a condo building.
Are the HOA dues deductible? It depends on how the home is used
How you use the home Deductible? What it means
You live in it all year No HOA fees on a home you live in are a personal cost, like your insurance and utilities.
A second home you never rent No The same rule as a main home. The dues are not deductible.
You rent it out and never stay there Yes, all All of the dues are a rental expense, including months it sits empty while you hold it out for rent (listed and open to bookings).
You rent it out and stay there some nights Partly You deduct the rented share of the dues, worked out by nights.
Your home, rented fewer than 15 days No You report no rent and deduct no rental costs.
You work from home Not for employees An employee gets no home office deduction. A self-employed owner who qualifies splits whole-home costs by the share used for business.

A deduction is not money back. It lowers the rental income that is taxed, and what it saves depends on the rest of your return.

## How much of the HOA fee can I deduct if I rent and use the condo?
You deduct the rented share: rented nights as a share of rented nights plus personal nights. Nights the condo sat empty count on neither side.
A night rented at a fair price counts as rented, even if you were there that day. A fair price is about what a person not related to you would pay. A rent far below what similar condos nearby charge is not a fair price.
Put in your own numbers:

Dues you deduct for the year $6,686
Rented share of the nights 86%
This condo counts as your home under the IRS test below, because your personal nights are more than 14. The figure above is the most you can deduct. It is cut if your rental costs are more than the rent.

Worked example: fewer personal nights can mean a larger deduction. On the condo below, rented 120 nights, cutting personal nights from 20 to 14 raises the deductible dues. The condo also stops counting as your home.
Example: deductible dues on one condo with $7,800 a year in dues How the condo is used, rented share dues you deduct

Lived in all year · a home: no deduction $0
Rented 120 nights, 20 personal nights · 86%; counts as your home $6,686
Rented 120 nights, 14 personal nights · 90%; not your home $6,985
Held for rent all year, no personal nights · all of the dues $7,800

The condo has the middle dues of Horry County condos for sale, $650 a month.

### When the condo counts as your home
The IRS counts a condo as your home if your personal nights are more than 14. If you rent it more than 140 nights at a fair price, the line is 10 percent of those nights instead.
Counting as your home matters when the rent is less than your rental costs. Then the deductions stop at the rent, and you can use the rest on next year's return for the same condo.
If it does not count as your home, the rental can show a loss. Whether that loss lowers the tax on your other income, such as wages, depends on the loss limits on our short-term rental tax page .
This IRS test is not the county's 72-day limit for the property tax rate, which comes below. The 14-day rule page has the other IRS day counts.

### What counts as a personal night
Counts as a personal night

- A night you or a co-owner stays there

- A night a relative stays, unless they rent it at a fair price as their main home

- A night anyone pays less than a fair rent

- A night someone stays in a swap that lets you use another home

Does not count as a personal night

- A night rented at a fair price, even if you were there that day

- A day you spend working close to full time on repairs and upkeep, even if family members enjoy the condo that day

Relatives are a spouse, brothers and sisters including half, parents, grandparents and earlier generations, and children, grandchildren and later generations. A day spent improving the condo, not repairing it, is not a repair day.

## What do condo HOA fees cost in Horry County?
About $650 a month, or $7,800 a year, for the middle condo for sale in Horry County. In oceanfront buildings the middle is about $925 a month. The middle dues are about $375 a month in Socastee and about $875 at the north end of Myrtle Beach.

On a rental, the insurance, utilities and internet are rental costs too, inside the dues or not.
The deduction needs nights you are allowed to rent. About 7 in 10 condos for sale in Horry County say they allow short-term rentals. When we search for a buyer who plans to rent, we filter out communities that ban renting. Then our agents read the rental rules in the HOA documents.

## Do HOA fees count as property tax?
No. HOA fees are not a property tax, because an association, not a government, charges them. The IRS says you cannot deduct them as real estate tax .
A home you live in, once you claim it with the county, is taxed at the 4 percent rate. Rentals, second homes and any home whose owner has not claimed that rate pay 6 percent. An owner who lives in another state pays 6 percent, because the 4 percent rate is only for the owner's domicile . To look up what the county bills a home, use our Horry County tax records guide .
On a Myrtle Beach condo at the 4 percent rate, a year of dues at the middle for condos for sale in ZIP 29577 is about $9,300. That is about 11 times the 2026 tax bill on a middle-valued condo in the city taxed at that rate, about $830.

Dues: the middle monthly dues of condos for sale in ZIP 29577 (Myrtle Beach) or 29582 (North Myrtle Beach), times 12. Tax: the 2026 county bill of the middle-valued condo at that rate in Myrtle Beach or North Myrtle Beach.
On a home you live in, the property tax counts on the federal return if you itemize, meaning you list your deductions instead of taking the standard deduction. The dues never do. On a rental, both are rental expenses.

### The county's 72-day limit
A condo you live in can be rented for part of the year and keep the 4 percent rate. It keeps that rate only while you still qualify and rent it no more than 72 days in a calendar year. The assessor may ask for your Schedule E.
The property tax page explains the two rates and works out the bill at either one.

## Is an HOA special assessment tax deductible?
On a rental, yes if it pays for upkeep, and slowly if it pays for an improvement. On a home you live in, no. A special assessment is a one-time bill on top of the dues, usually for a large job.
Is a special assessment deductible?
Rental, for upkeep
Deductible the year you pay it An assessment for upkeep of the shared parts is a rental expense, like the dues.

Rental, for an improvement
Spread over 27.5 years You deduct a share each year, starting when the work is finished and ready to use. The IRS calls this depreciation.

Your home, for upkeep
Not deductible An assessment for upkeep on a home you live in gives no deduction.

Your condo, for an improvement
Added to your cost basis It gives no deduction the year you pay it. It lowers the taxable gain when you sell.

Worked example: your share of a roof assessment on a condo you rent out is $10,000. You deduct about $364 a year in each full year, over 27.5 years from when the new roof is in service. In service means finished and ready to use.
A $10,000 roof assessment on a condo you rent out, spread over the years

- $10,000 your share of the roof, paid to the association

- 27.5 years the period the IRS uses for a rental home and its roof

- about $364 deducted in each full year; the first and last years are less

Our page on rental depreciation shows how the first and last years are counted.
On a condo you live in, an assessment that is not just for repairs or upkeep is added to your cost basis, what the home cost you. The basis rarely matters on a main home. If you qualify, the first $250,000 of gain is not taxed, or $500,000 for a married couple filing jointly.
Whether a job is upkeep or an improvement depends on the work. The assessment notice and the board's minutes say what the work is.

## Does South Carolina treat HOA fees differently?
No. South Carolina starts from the federal figures , so the same rules on dues, rental days and depreciation apply on the state return. From 2026, South Carolina does not use the federal itemized deductions. That does not touch the dues on a rental, which come off the rent, not off a list of itemized deductions.
About 6 in 10 Horry County condo units have their tax bill mailed to an address outside South Carolina. For an owner who lives in another state, the rent from a Grand Strand condo, less its costs and dues, is South Carolina income.
On the South Carolina return, the dues come off that rent the same way they do on the federal return. How your home state treats the same rent depends on that state's law, not South Carolina's.

## Where do HOA fees go on Schedule E, and what records do I keep?
Schedule E has no line for association dues. An expense not listed on lines 5 to 18 goes on line 19, Other .
Line 2 asks for the nights rented at a fair price and the nights of personal use. Keep these four records:

- 1 The association's statements They show what you paid in dues and in any special assessment, and when.

- 2 A log of nights Write down each night rented at a fair price, each personal night and each repair day, as they happen.

- 3 The assessment notice and the minutes They say what an assessment paid for, which decides whether it is upkeep or an improvement.

- 4 The two night counts Give them to whoever prepares your return. Schedule E asks for both.

The HOA documents page lists what each paper shows. What you pay the association at closing is on our page on transfer fees .

Common questions

## HOA fees and taxes FAQ

### Are HOA fees tax deductible on my primary residence?
No. On a home you live in, HOA and condo fees are a personal cost, like insurance and utilities. They are not a property tax either, because an association, not a government, charges them.

### Are HOA fees deductible on a rental property?
Yes. On a condo you rent out, the dues are a rental expense on Schedule E. On a house in an HOA that you rent out, the dues are a cost of renting it, like insurance and repairs.

### Are HOA fees deductible on a second home I do not rent?
No. A second home you never rent follows the same rule as a main home. If you rent it for 15 days or more, the rented share of the nights becomes deductible.

### Can I deduct HOA fees if I work from home?
Not as an employee: an employee gets no home office deduction. A self-employed owner who qualifies splits whole-home costs by the share of the home used for business. The IRS's examples are insurance, utilities and general repairs. Its home office guide does not say whether association dues count, so this page does not say they do.

### Do HOA special assessments lower capital gains when I sell?
On a condo you live in, an assessment for an improvement is added to your cost basis, which lowers the taxable gain. If you qualify, the first $250,000 of gain on a main home is not taxed, or $500,000 for a married couple filing jointly.

### Do family stays count as personal use?
Yes, unless the relative rents it at a fair price as their main home. A stay by you, a co-owner or a relative is a personal night, and so is any night rented below a fair price.
Sources: IRS Pub. 527 , IRS Pub. 530 , IRS Pub. 523 , IRS Pub. 587 , Schedule E instructions , SC Code 12-6 , SC Code 12-37 , SC Code 12-43 , SC Act 110 (H. 4216) , Horry County Treasurer . ## How Much Can an HOA Raise Dues in SC? | Chapter3
URL: https://chapter3realty.com/hoa/dues-increases/
Summary: South Carolina puts no cap on an HOA dues increase, and the notice you get is short. What limits it, and what to read before you offer.

Home / HOA Guide / Dues Increases
Dues increases

# How much an HOA can raise your dues in South Carolina
By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge, 30+ years on the Grand Strand · Updated November 12, 2026
South Carolina does not cap HOA dues increases, by percent or by dollar. The limit on your increase is in your community's recorded documents. Read them before you offer.
Have us read the budget Call 854.333.2135

THE STATE RULE

## State law sets no cap on dues
Start with the short answer. State law puts no cap on a dues increase. There is no percent limit, no dollar limit, and no tie to inflation. The only thing state law says about raising a budget is that owners get notice first.
That notice is at least forty eight hours before the meeting where the budget goes up. Two days. Watch where it lands. It runs to the meeting, not to the decision, and not to the day your bill changes. It can be a sign in a common area, a post on the association website, an email, or any method set in the bylaws.
The rule also misses a lot of associations. Many here are set up as nonprofit corporations, and the two day rule does not apply to them. They follow their own bylaws instead, which usually give members more warning of a meeting. But your budget may be set by the board with no owner meeting at all. The recorded documents say which.

WHAT LIMITS IT

## Your recorded documents set the real limit
Your association's documents bind you only if they were recorded in the county land records. That is good news for a buyer. The papers that control a dues increase are public, so you can read them before you make an offer.
In a condo, you owe a share of the shared costs, and the share for each unit is fixed. You cannot lower it by skipping the pool or the elevator. Outside a condo, state law gives you less than people expect. No cap. No vote threshold. No collection rules. If your community has any of those, the recorded declaration created them. If the declaration has none, nothing limits how big an increase can be.
Read the declaration for five things before you offer. Send us the address of the unit and we read all five and tell you what they say.

- &#10003; A yearly cap. Some documents set the most a board can add without an owner vote. Check whether it runs off last year or off a fixed base year.

- &#10003; A vote threshold. Check what share of owners has to approve an increase above the cap, and whether that share is all owners or only the ones who vote.

- &#10003; Costs left outside the cap. Insurance, utilities and taxes are often carved out. On this coast that one carve out can make a cap useless.

- &#10003; Who sets the budget. Check whether the board adopts it alone or owners approve it, and what notice the bylaws require.

- &#10003; Builder rules. Check whether one class of members votes differently while the builder still runs the association.

Have us read the budget Call 854.333.2135

WHY THEY GO UP HERE

## Insurance and lender rules push budgets up
We do not publish a reason for any one association's increase, and we do not guess at it. What is true across this coast is that insuring older oceanfront buildings has become expensive and hard to arrange. Insurance is usually the largest line in a coastal condo budget. When it renews higher, the dues follow.
Lenders push from the other side. Most now look at two things: how much of an insurance claim each owner could be charged under the building policy, and how much of the yearly dues goes into savings for big repairs. Both have tightened. An association that wants its units to stay easy to finance has to pay for both, and that lands in the budget your dues fund.
This matters even if you pay cash. When a building stops meeting what lenders want, buyers there cannot get loans, the pool of buyers shrinks, and that shows up in your resale price. Ask for the latest insurance renewal and the reserve line in the budget. Send us both and we read them with you.

BEFORE YOU CLOSE

## What to settle before you close
The papers that would show an increase coming already exist. The only question is whether you see them in time to act on them. Ask on day one. Associations and their managers often take about three days to release documents, and some take longer. Build that into your dates.
The right to demand association records belongs to owners, and a buyer under contract is not an owner yet. Your route is the contract and the seller. Put document delivery and a review window in the contract, in writing, with a deadline. This is general information and not legal advice. For a dispute, talk to a South Carolina attorney.
Two charges surprise buyers late. A special assessment is not a dues increase. It is a one time charge for one cost, and state law sets no notice period for it at all. Back dues attach to the unit rather than to the person. If the seller owes money, you owe it once you buy. In a condo the association has to hand a buyer a written statement of what is owed, but only if the buyer asks. Ask in writing, get that payoff figure before closing, and you owe no more than the figure on the statement.
Have us read the budget Call 854.333.2135

WHAT TO GET

## Get these documents before you offer
Expect the association to charge you something at closing on top of the dues. A few months of dues up front is common, and so is a document fee and a fee to open your account. No state law caps those amounts, so have the seller get the figure from the association early.
Then get the six items below. Send them to us the day they arrive. We read the declaration, the budget, the reserve study , the insurance renewal and the minutes, then tell you the limit on an increase, what sits outside that limit, and what the last three budgets did.

- &#10003; This year's budget and the two before it. A three year trend tells you more than any single year.

- &#10003; The reserve line in the budget, plus the reserve study if one has been done.

- &#10003; Board and owner meeting minutes for the last twelve months. Insurance renewals and big repair bills show up here first.

- &#10003; The current insurance certificate and the terms of the latest renewal.

- &#10003; The recorded declaration and bylaws, read for a cap, a vote threshold and any cost left outside the cap.

- &#10003; In a condo, the written statement of what is owed on the unit. Ask for it, because it is only given on request.

Common questions

## Dues Increases FAQ

### How much notice does an HOA have to give before raising dues in South Carolina?
At least forty eight hours before the meeting where the budget goes up. That is two days, and the notice runs to the meeting, not to the increase itself. It can be a sign, a website post, an email, or any method the bylaws allow. Nonprofit associations follow their own bylaws instead.

### Is there a limit on how much an HOA can raise dues in SC?
No. Neither the HOA law nor the condo law sets a maximum. There is no percent limit and no dollar limit. Any limit on your association sits in the recorded declaration and bylaws. Read them for a cap, for the vote it takes to go above that cap, and for costs allowed to rise outside it.

### Does South Carolina require 14 days notice before an HOA raises dues?
No. Two days is the figure in state law. The longer numbers come from bills that were introduced and never passed, and in one of those the fourteen days was notice of a hearing about a rule violation, not a dues increase. Your bylaws may promise you more.

### Can an HOA raise dues without a vote of the owners?
State law does not require one. Nothing in the HOA law or the condo law makes an increase depend on an owner vote. Whether a vote is needed, and at what share, comes from the recorded declaration and bylaws. In a condo the bylaws have to state that share.

### Why are HOA dues going up in Myrtle Beach?
We do not guess at one association's reason. Across this coast, insuring older oceanfront buildings has become expensive and hard to arrange, and insurance is usually the biggest line in a condo budget. Lenders also want more money going into reserves. Read the budget and the insurance renewal.

## Best Time to Sell a House in Myrtle Beach: List in March

# The best time to sell a house in Myrtle Beach List in March to close in May or June.

- March to June about 38 percent of a year's home sales

By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge · Updated November 8, 2026
The best time to list, from five years of Horry County deed records month by month, with the weeks from listing to closing.

The short answer
The best time to sell a house in Myrtle Beach is late spring and early summer. Homes that closed in June sold for a middle price about 6 percent above homes that closed in February. About 38 percent of a year's home sales here are recorded in March through June.
To close in those months, list a house in March and a condo in late January or February. This spring, a home had a buyer after about 6 to 7 weeks on the market. Closing took about 5 weeks more.
The month is worth a few percent of the price. The year you sell in and the price you ask can matter more.

## When do the most homes sell in Myrtle Beach?
Spring and early summer are the busiest months for home sales in Horry County. From 2021 to 2025, about 38 percent of home resales were recorded in March through June. That is more than in any other four months in a row. An even spread would be 33 percent.

Horry County, the five years added together, from our count of county deeds. Resales only: builders' sales of new homes are left out. March to June, the four busiest months, are in color.
January and February are the slowest months. Together they hold about 13 percent of a year's sales.
The pattern is not the same every year. In 2025, sales were spread more evenly, and October was the busiest month. Prices still followed the season that year. February was again the lowest month for price, and houses that closed in June and July still sold above the months around them.

### Which month brings the highest price?
June brought the highest middle price, and February the lowest. Half of the homes sold for more than the middle price, and half for less.
February was lower than the months around it in all five years. May and June were higher in four of the five.

From February's bar to June's bar is about 6 percent. On a home at the county's middle resale price of about $305,000, that is about $20,000. Part of that gap comes from which homes sell in each month, so one home should expect less. We could not measure how much less.

## When should you list to close in the best months?
List about three months before the month you want to close. A home is under contract, which agents call pending, once the buyer and the seller have both signed the purchase contract.
Homes go under contract fastest in March, April and May. This spring, the middle home had a buyer after about 6 to 7 weeks on the market. In the years before, it was about 4 weeks.
After a buyer signs, closing took about five weeks here, in every month of the year. A buyer who pays cash has no lender to wait for. Our page on cash offers covers that kind of sale.

## Is the best month different for a condo?
Yes. Condos here sell for the most in April and May, a little earlier in the year than houses, which sell for the most in June.

- A condo Close in April or May. List in late January or February. Condos that closed in April and May sold for the highest middle prices of the year, about 9 percent above February's.
If you rent the condo by the night, a spring sale gives up the summer. In all eight towns in our rental data, nightly rentals earn the most in July.
Renting through the summer and selling in the fall has a cost too. Condos that closed from September to November sold for about the same as the months around them, not the spring high.

- A house or townhome Close in June. List in March. Houses that closed in June sold for the highest middle price of the year, about 5 percent above February's.
July and September closings did nearly as well. All three months were above the months around them in all five years.

Our page on selling a condo covers the rest of a condo sale: the HOA papers, rental programs and buyers' loans.

## Is winter a bad time to sell a house in Myrtle Beach?
Winter has fewer sales and lower prices. It also has fewer homes for sale to compete with yours.

- Fewer sales, lower prices January and February have the fewest sales of the year. February closings sold for the lowest middle price of the year.

- Fewer homes for sale In the Myrtle Beach area, December has the fewest new listings of the year, less than half of April's. Buyers still sign contracts all winter, about 640 in a typical December.

- Out-of-state buyers buy all year About 3 in 10 buyers in every month are from another state. Our page on out-of-state buyers says where they come from.

A home that goes under contract in February closes about five weeks later, in March or early April, when the busy months begin.

## Does hurricane season hurt a home sale here?
Not as a season. Atlantic hurricane season is June 1 to November 30. Most of the season's activity comes between mid-August and mid-October, with the peak on September 10.
Those months are not a slow season for home sales. August, September and October each had about 8 to 9 percent of a year's home resales. August and September closings sold a little above the months around them on average.

### What happened to home sales the week Hurricane Ian came?
Hurricane Ian came ashore near Georgetown on Friday, September 30, 2022. The county recorded no home sales that day. It recorded sales again the next Monday, and the week after the storm had more sales than the week before.

## Do tourist season and the school year change the best month?
Tourist season peaks in July, after the busiest months for home sales. School lets out in early June, during one of them.
Photo: Loadmaster
Myrtle Beach on a June day. Tourist season peaks in July, the month after houses here sell highest.

- Tourist season This year, Horry County had about 40 percent more hotel, restaurant and other leisure jobs in July than in January. Home sales do not follow the tourists: July has fewer sales than June.

- The school year Horry County public schools let out in early June and start again in mid-August. This school year ends on June 8, 2027, and the next one starts on August 18, 2027. Make-up days can move the last day.

- Moving while school is out June is one of the two busiest months for home sales. To close in June, list in March.

## What matters more than the month you sell?
Prices changed far more from year to year than from month to month. The middle price rose about 20 percent from 2021 to 2022, against about 6 percent between February and June.

- The year Since 2024 the middle resale price has stayed near $305,000. So far this year it has been about the same again, with about as many sales as a year earlier. Our home value page gives middle prices by area.

- The market now In September 2026, about 8,000 homes were for sale in the Myrtle Beach area, about the same as a year earlier. Homes went under contract about a week faster than a year earlier.

- The asking price That month, about 3 in 10 listings had cut their asking price. Each week a home waits for a cut moves its closing a week later, and can push a spring closing into summer. Buyers paid about 97 to 98 percent of the last asking price, whatever the month. The row of just-listed homes on this page shows what yours would compete with.

- Tax dates Owning and living in your main home for 2 of the last 5 years can mean no federal tax on up to $250,000 of your profit. If you are a few months short, selling early can cost that. A rental or second home has its own one-year date. Our capital gains page explains both, from IRS Topic 701 and IRS Topic 409 . Ask a tax pro about your own dates.

- Your own dates You may have a date you must move by: a lease that ends, a new job, or a home you are buying. Work back from that date with the weeks above. Our pages on whether to sell or buy first and selling a rented home cover those cases.

## Best time to sell FAQ

### What is the worst month to sell a house in Myrtle Beach?
February. For houses and for condos alike, it was the lowest month of the year for price, and one of the slowest for sales.

### Do houses sell in December in Myrtle Beach?
Yes. Buyers sign contracts all winter. A contract signed in December closes about five weeks later, in January.

### How long does it take from contract to closing in Myrtle Beach?
About five weeks. The average ran from 36 days to 42 days, depending on the month.

### Is now a good time to sell a house in Myrtle Beach?
At this year's pace, a home listed in mid November closes around mid February, the lowest month for price. Listing in March moves the closing to May or June, at the cost of four more months of owning the home.

### When is the best time to sell a beach condo in Myrtle Beach?
Close in April or May, when condos sold for the most. That means listing in late January or February, before the summer rental season.

How we counted. We read the county's index of every deed recorded since 2019 and counted 65,664 home resales from 2021 to 2025. A resale is a deed of $10,000 or more for one home that the county lists today as residential, with a building on it.
We left out 21,968 sales by builders, whose closings are spread more evenly over the year. We also left out tax sales, foreclosures, corrective deeds and sales under 30 percent of the county's value.
Of the 65,664 resales, about 37,400 were houses and townhomes and 28,300 condos. We told a condo from a house by the county's parcel records.
Each sale is counted in the month the county recorded its deed, which comes after the closing. The county's index carries a parcel number on nearly every deed only from July 2020, so our count starts in 2021. ## Myrtle Beach Cash Offers: Flippers Paid 68% of Resale Price
URL: https://chapter3realty.com/sell/cash-offer/
Summary: What companies paid for Horry County houses against what they resold for, how long a listing takes, when a cash offer makes sense, and how to check one.

Home / Sell / Cash Offer or List
Selling a home

# A cash offer for your Myrtle Beach house, or list it? House flippers here paid about 68 percent of the price they resold for.

- About 68% what flippers here paid, of the price they resold for

- At least 1 in 3 home resales here had no home loan recorded

By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge · Updated November 8, 2026
What cash buyers in Horry County paid against what they resold for, when cash is the better choice, and how to check the buyer and the contract.

The short answer
List it, unless the house needs heavy repairs, cannot get a loan or insurance, or must be sold by a fixed date. Then a cash offer can be the better choice.
Companies that bought Horry County houses from their owners and resold them within a year paid about 68 cents for each dollar of the resale price. That is the middle sale: half paid more, half paid less. On a house worth $260,000 fixed up, that is an offer of about $178,000.
A cash sale skips the wait for a loan. In September 2026, the middle listed home in the Myrtle Beach area took 53 days to get a signed contract, then about five weeks to close.

## Who makes cash offers on houses in Myrtle Beach?
Three kinds of buyer make cash offers on houses here:

- Online instant-offer buyers A company that makes an offer online from the address, also called an iBuyer.

- Local investors People and companies who buy a house to fix up and resell, or to rent out.

- "We buy houses" buyers Buyers who send letters, call, or put up roadside signs offering cash for houses. We check them the same way as any other buyer.

Many more buyers here pay without a home loan. We matched the county's deed and mortgage records for a full year of home resales. At least 1 in 3 had no new home loan recorded in the buyer's name, and about 3 in 4 of those buyers were people, not companies. A house listed for sale reaches those buyers too.

## How much less is a cash offer, and how do cash buyers set the price?
In the middle sale, a company paid about a third less than it later resold the house for.
The chart shows the middle prices. Companies paid $170,000 for houses they bought from the owners, and resold them for $260,000, about four months later.

A company that buys to resell has to pay for repairs, months of holding the house, two closings and the costs of selling. It pays for all of them, and its profit, out of the difference between the two prices. Offers vary from house to house.

## Cash offer or listing: which leaves you more money?
Listing leaves you more when repairs, fees and time cost less than the cash buyer's discount. Take a house that would sell for $260,000 once fixed up, the middle resale price in our count. A cash offer at the middle share companies paid would be about $178,000.
Three ways to sell a house that would bring $260,000 fixed up How you sell What it sells for Repairs you pay for Listing fees
Take the cash offer About $178,000 None None
List it as is Its as-is price (we work it out) None $1,780 for each 1% at $178,000
Fix it, then list it Up to about $260,000 Yours to pay, and the months they take $2,600 for each 1%

Listing fees are a percent you agree with your agent. When each way beats the cash offer:

- List it as is It leaves you more when its price, less the listing fees, is above the offer. Our count of the county's deeds cannot tell a house sold as it is from one that was fixed up, so it gives no as-is price. We work that price out for your house from the recorded sales near it.

- Fix it, then list it It leaves you more when the repairs and the listing fees come to less than about $82,000.

This is an example on the county's middle figures, not an offer on any house.

## When is a cash offer the better choice?
A cash offer is the better choice when a buyer with a loan cannot buy the house, or when you need a sure closing date.
A cash sale has no lender, so there is no loan approval or lender's appraisal to wait for. A South Carolina attorney still supervises the title search, the closing and the recording of the deed. Our page on the best time to sell shows how the wait for a contract changes by month.
When a cash offer is the better choice If this is your house The better choice
It has damage to its safety or structure A cash buyer, or a listing marked cash only. Until the damage is repaired, a buyer cannot get a home loan on it that Fannie Mae will buy from the lender. Fannie Mae is the company that buys many home loans from the lenders that make them, so lenders follow its rules.
No insurer will cover it for wind A cash buyer. A home loan backed by Fannie Mae needs insurance that covers wind , hurricanes included. Our coastal insurance page covers wind policies here.
It must be sold by a date: a move, an estate or a divorce Set a firm cash closing date beside a listing priced to sell. Our pages on an inherited house and on selling in a divorce cover the rest.
A tenant has months left on the lease List it in front of investors who buy rented houses. Our rental property page covers selling with a tenant.
It is in fair shape, and you have time to sell List it, as it is or fixed up.

## Can you sell a house as is in South Carolina?
Yes. "As is" means you sell without making repairs. The state's disclosure form is still required, and a cash sale is not exempt for being cash. Our page on the seller disclosure form goes through it question by question.

### Sellers already list houses as cash only
A seller can list the house as it is and ask for cash buyers only. The local listing feed had these:
Listed as cash only on November 8, 2026

- 22 houses

- 105 condos

- 55 manufactured homes

Listings on CCMLS, the local agents' listing service, counted on our site.

A cash offer made before the house is listed is one buyer's offer. A listing puts the house in front of every buyer at once, with a loan or without. The state Real Estate Commission warns that keeping a home off the open market can mean less competition and a lower price, worse terms or a longer sale.

### One sale to a cash buyer
One of our agents sold a rented house this way. The owner was moving to New York to be with his sister, and the lease still had eight months left. The next investor would make only about half his monthly cash flow, the rent left after costs, because of higher taxes and a bigger loan.
The agent marketed the house to our list of investors who accept a modest cash flow on a home rising in value. A cash buyer closed within 13 days of the day it was listed. That was his sale and his figures, not a promise. Our rental property page tells the rest.

## How do you check a cash buyer and the contract?
Before you sign a cash buyer's contract, our agents check six things:

- Proof of the money A recent bank statement or a letter from the buyer's bank that shows the cash. We ask for it before you sign.

- The deposit The buyer's good-faith deposit is called earnest money. A third party, such as an attorney, holds it until closing. If the buyer walks away for a reason the contract does not allow, the seller may keep it. Across the US , no law requires a deposit, and deposits typically run 1 to 10 percent of the price.

- The inspection period If the contract makes the sale depend on an inspection , the buyer can back out of the sale. A buyer who walks away because a condition of the contract was not met gets the deposit back. A long inspection period with a small deposit means the buyer can back out late at little cost while the house is under contract.

- Any right to hand the contract on The words "and/or assigns" after the buyer's name let the buyer pass its place in your contract to someone else. That is not wholesaling by itself. It becomes wholesaling when the buyer also markets your house before owning it.

- Who the buyer is We look the company up by name in the Secretary of State's business records , where every South Carolina LLC and corporation is filed.

- The closing Every South Carolina home closing, cash or loan, must be supervised by a South Carolina attorney.

Wire fraud. Never follow wiring instructions in an email. Confirm them in person or by phone with the attorney's office, at a number you agreed on in advance.

### Is wholesaling legal in South Carolina?
No, as the state Real Estate Commission reads the law. Since May 2024, South Carolina's license law has defined wholesaling. It means having a contract to buy a home from its owner, then marketing it to a different buyer before owning it.

- Marketing takes a license Marketing a home someone else owns, for pay, takes a real estate license. In its advisory opinion , the Commission reads that as a ban on wholesaling.

- What counts as marketing The MLS, social media, email groups and word of mouth. Naming the address, a photo or the neighborhood counts too.

- Brokerages A licensed brokerage such as Chapter3 may not take part in wholesaling or help anyone do it.

The Commission's opinion is guidance, not a court ruling. If a buyer markets your house before closing, a South Carolina attorney can tell you what it means for your contract.
Got a contract from a cash buyer?
Send it to us before you sign. Our agents read the deposit, the inspection period and any right to hand it on, and tell you what each means for you.

## Cash offer FAQ

### Do you pay closing costs in a cash sale?
Yes, at least the state and county deed fee. The seller owes it by law in a cash sale or a listed one: $1.85 for each $500 of the price, about $659 on $178,000. A contract can shift who pays it. Our net proceeds calculator adds the other costs.

### Can a cash buyer skip the seller disclosure form?

## South Carolina Seller Disclosure: All 28 Questions
URL: https://chapter3realty.com/sell/seller-disclosure/
Summary: What South Carolina sellers must disclose: all 28 questions on the state form, who is exempt, flooding, the beachfront rule and lead paint.

Home / Sell / Seller Disclosure
Selling a home

# South Carolina seller disclosure: all 28 questions What the state form asks, who is exempt, and the extra papers some homes need.

- 28 questions on the state form, each Yes, No or No Representation

- 8 items ask about the years you owned the home

- 15 kinds of sale need no form

By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge · Updated November 14, 2026
Who must fill in the state form, what its 28 numbered questions mean, and what happens if a seller leaves something out.

The short answer
A South Carolina seller must give the buyer the state's disclosure form, filled in and signed, before both sign the contract. The form asks what you know about the home, and a seller who knowingly leaves a problem off can owe the buyer their losses.
Fifteen kinds of sale need no form. Two things touch many Grand Strand sales. One is the flood questions about the years you owned the home. The other is a beachfront statement for homes on lots past the state's setback line, about 10,700 in Horry County.
